idiom_name: Rails ActionDispatch session (CookieStore default; ActiveRecord/Redis stores)
implementation_notes: Rails provides a per-request session hash through ActionDispatch, so the manager role is the middleware plus the chosen store. The default CookieStore encrypts and signs the whole payload with keys derived from secret_key_base and keeps no server-side record; server-side stores (ActiveRecordStore, Redis) keep the identifier and make sessions revocable. The fixation defence is the one-line reset_session, which issues a new identifier and drops the old data, and the Rails 8 authentication generator adds a server-side Session model with ip_address and user_agent columns for exactly the revocable case.
code_sketch:
class SessionsController < ApplicationController
  def create
    user = User.authenticate_by(params.permit(:email_address, :password))
    reset_session                       # new identifier: session fixation defence
    session[:user_id] = user.id
    redirect_to after_authentication_url
  end
  def destroy
    reset_session                       # revoke server-side record and cookie
    redirect_to new_session_url
  end
end
pitfalls: CookieStore is not invalidated on logout: the documentation states a copied cookie remains usable until it ages out, so it must not hold security-critical state.
The 4 KB cookie limit and the payload travelling on every request make CookieStore unsuitable for large or fast-changing session state.
Rotating secret_key_base expires every active session (documented behaviour), so key rotation is an all-users logout and needs a plan.
Storing derived values (credits, entitlements) in the session enables replay attacks by reusing an older cookie; keep authoritative data in the database.
